title: Accessible information, sensory impairment and interpreters
blurb: Apply the Accessible Information Standard, support people with sensory impairment and use interpreters safely.
question: A woman who speaks little English attends for a pre-operative assessment with her 12-year-old son, who offers to interpret. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: People can only make informed decisions if they can access and understand information. Code 7.2 asks you to take reasonable steps to meet people's language and communication needs. In England, the Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605) is a legal requirement for organisations providing NHS care or publicly funded adult social care, for people with a disability, impairment or sensory loss, and their carers and parents.
teach.cite: NMC Code 7.2; NHS England AIS (issued under s250 Health and Social Care Act 2012, updated 2025)

teach.h: The Accessible Information Standard: six steps
teach.caption: Record the NEED (for example 'requires BSL interpreter'), not just the diagnosis.

teach.body: Offer a professional interpreter whenever someone needs language support. If the person prefers a family member or friend, seek and record their consent to this independently of the relative. Using children under 16 to interpret is unacceptable, except to get immediate, necessary treatment. Family interpreters may filter information, lack medical vocabulary and compromise confidentiality.
teach.cite: NHS England, Guidance for commissioners: interpreting and translation services (2018)

children.label: Professional interpreter
children.sub: face to face, video or phone

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Ama in a pre-assessment clinic
teach.body: Mrs Rahimi speaks Dari and little English; her 12-year-old son offers to interpret. Ama thanks him but books a professional Dari interpreter by video, explaining this ensures accurate information and privacy. She records Mrs Rahimi's language and interpreter need on the system so it is visible at her admission. She checks understanding with teach-back through the interpreter.

teach.h: Supporting sensory impairment and communication aids
items: Check hearing aids are in, switched on and working, and glasses are clean and worn.
For lipreading: face the person, good light on your face, speak clearly at normal pace.
Use alternative techniques where needed: writing, pictures, communication boards, signing.
Use repetition and positive reinforcement to support understanding (Annexe A 2.6).
Make reasonable adjustments, such as longer appointments (Equality Act s20).

teach.caption: Spoken language needs that are not related to disability are outside the AIS, but should still be recorded and met.

teach.text: The AIS covers needs arising from DISABILITY, IMPAIRMENT OR SENSORY LOSS. A need for a spoken language interpreter for someone who does not speak English is outside its scope, yet Code 7.2 still requires you to meet it.

items: AIS six steps: identify, record, flag, share, meet, review.
Applies to NHS and publicly funded adult social care, for patients, carers and parents.
Use professional interpreters; record consent if a relative interprets; not children under 16.
Check aids, adapt your communication and use repetition and reinforcement.

summary: You can now apply the six steps of the Accessible Information Standard and choose formats and support to match people's needs. You can also use interpreters safely and support people with sensory impairment and communication aids.

A.q: What is the first step of the Accessible Information Standard?
options: Record the person's needs
Identify the person's needs
Flag the person's needs
Meet the person's needs
A.why: The AIS steps are identify (ask), record, flag, share, meet and review.

whyNot.0: Recording comes after identifying the needs.

A.q: A patient who is Deaf uses British Sign Language. Her appointment letter asks her to phone the clinic. Under the AIS, what should happen?
options: Ask a relative to make telephone calls on her behalf
Send her future letters in large print instead
Record and flag her need for text contact and BSL
Ask her to bring a hearing friend to appointments
A.why: The AIS requires her communication needs to be identified, recorded, flagged and met, including accessible contact methods and a BSL interpreter.

whyNot.0: Relying on relatives does not meet her own communication needs.
whyNot.1: Large print does not address being unable to use the phone.
whyNot.3: Expecting her to bring someone shifts the duty onto her.

A.q: A patient's son offers to interpret for his mother at her outpatient appointment. She agrees. What should the nurse do?
options: Offer a professional and record her consent independently
Accept his offer, as family members know her best
Decline, as relatives may not interpret in the NHS
Carry on in English and check understanding with gestures
A.why: A professional interpreter should be offered. If she prefers a family member, her consent should be sought and recorded independently of the relative (NHS England 2018).

whyNot.1: Family members may filter information; her consent must be confirmed independently.
whyNot.2: Adult relatives can interpret if the person consents after a professional is offered.
whyNot.3: Gestures alone do not meet her language needs.

B.q: A 10-year-old girl offers to interpret for her father during a discussion about his cancer treatment. What is most appropriate?
options: Accept, as she speaks both languages fluently
Let her interpret the simpler questions
Accept if her father gives consent
Arrange a professional interpreter
B.why: Using children under 16 to interpret is unacceptable except to obtain immediate necessary treatment. A cancer treatment discussion needs a professional interpreter.

whyNot.0: Fluency does not make it acceptable to place a child in this role.
whyNot.1: Even simple questions risk distress and inaccurate information.
whyNot.2: The father's consent does not make using a child acceptable here.

B.q: An older man with hearing loss seems confused during a discussion. What should the nurse check first?
options: Whether his hearing aids are in and working
His cognition using a screening tool
Whether he needs a sedative
His blood glucose level
B.why: Supporting personal communication aids is a core skill (Annexe A 2.4). Hearing aids not in or not working are a common, correctable cause of apparent confusion.

whyNot.1: Cognitive screening may be needed later, but a hearing problem should be excluded first.
whyNot.2: Sedation is not a response to communication difficulty.
whyNot.3: Glucose matters if confusion persists, but checking his aids is the immediate step.

B.q: Which need falls outside the scope of the Accessible Information Standard?
options: Easy read information for a person with a learning disability
A deafblind interpreter for a patient
A Polish interpreter for a person who does not speak English
Large print letters for a carer with sight loss
B.why: The AIS excludes spoken language needs that are not related to disability, although they should still be recorded and met under Code 7.2.

whyNot.0: Easy read for a learning disability is within scope.
whyNot.1: Deafblind communication support is within scope.
whyNot.3: Carers' needs related to sight loss are within scope.

C.q: A man with a learning disability is offered a standard leaflet before a colonoscopy. He says he cannot read well. What best meets the law and the AIS?
options: Ask his carer to read it to him later
Provide easy read information and record his need
Postpone the procedure until he can read it
Explain verbally and ask him to sign the consent form
C.why: The AIS requires his need to be identified, recorded and met, and the Equality Act s20(6) requires information in an accessible format as a reasonable adjustment.

whyNot.0: This passes responsibility to the carer and does not record or meet his need.
whyNot.2: Postponing does not adjust the format; it delays care.
whyNot.3: Verbal explanation may help, but without accessible information and checked understanding consent may not be informed.

C.q: A patient lipreads. Which approach best supports communication?
options: Speak loudly and exaggerate each word
Stand with the window light behind you
Wear a mask and speak slowly
Face her in good light and speak clearly
C.why: Lipreading needs a clear view of the speaker's face in good light, with clear speech at a normal pace (Annexe A 2.3).

whyNot.0: Shouting and exaggerating distort lip shapes.
whyNot.1: Light behind you puts your face in shadow.
whyNot.2: A standard mask hides the lips.

C.q: A woman with sight loss is the main carer for her husband, who is being discharged. Under the AIS, what should the ward do?
options: Identify, record and meet her information needs too
Give the discharge information to the patient instead
Post the discharge letter in standard print
Phone their GP to explain the plan
C.why: The AIS covers carers as well as patients: their needs should be identified, recorded (with consent where possible) and met.

whyNot.1: The carer needs information she can use as well.
whyNot.2: Standard print does not meet her need.
whyNot.3: Informing the GP does not give the carer accessible information.

reteach.title: Ask, write it down, wave a flag, pass it on, do it, check again
reteach.question: Can you walk the six AIS steps with one patient?

blocks.body: At admission you ASK Mr Jones about communication: he is partially sighted (identify). You WRITE it in his record as 'needs 16-point large print' (record). An alert appears when his record opens (flag). His referral to the physio includes it (share). His discharge letter arrives in large print (meet). At follow-up you ask if anything has changed (review).

blocks.text: Record the NEED ('requires a BSL interpreter'), not only the condition ('deaf'). Not every Deaf person uses BSL.

explain.body: A legal standard for NHS and publicly funded adult social care: identify, record, flag, share, meet and review the communication needs of people with disability, impairment or sensory loss.

test.q: Who must follow the Accessible Information Standard?
options: Private dental practices with no NHS patients
High street pharmacies for their retail sales
Providers of NHS or publicly funded adult social care
Charities providing services with no public funding
test.why: The AIS applies to organisations that provide NHS care or publicly funded adult social care.

whyNot.0: Purely private services are outside the AIS.
whyNot.1: Retail sales are not NHS care.
whyNot.3: Charities are covered only when providing NHS or publicly funded adult social care.

explain.body: Offer professional interpreters. If a relative is preferred, seek and record consent independently. Children under 16 only for immediate necessary treatment.

test.q: When is it acceptable to use a child under 16 as an interpreter?
options: For routine follow-up appointments
When the parent prefers it
When the child is fluent and willing
To obtain immediate necessary treatment
test.why: NHS England guidance: using children under 16 to interpret is unacceptable except to obtain immediate necessary treatment.

whyNot.0: Routine care allows time to book a professional.
whyNot.1: Parental preference does not make it acceptable.
whyNot.2: Fluency and willingness do not make it acceptable.

explain.body: Check aids are working, face the person, use good light, and offer alternative formats such as large print, audio or braille.

test.q: A partially sighted patient needs to read her medicines information. Which is an appropriate format?
options: Standard print with a magnifying lens
Large print in her preferred size
A video with subtitles
Information sent to her neighbour
test.why: Large print in the size she needs is a recognised accessible format under the AIS.

whyNot.0: This may help, but the AIS asks for the format she needs.
whyNot.2: Subtitles rely on vision and suit hearing loss rather than sight loss.
whyNot.3: Sending to a neighbour breaches confidentiality.

explain.body: Repeat key points, use simple language and praise progress to support people who need more time to understand.

test.q: A man with a learning disability is learning to use a spacer device. Which technique best reinforces his learning?
options: Repeat the steps and praise each success
Give him every step in one long explanation
Ask his support worker to do it for him
Leave a printed leaflet with medical terms
test.why: Repetition and positive reinforcement support understanding and confidence (Annexe A 2.6).

whyNot.1: One long explanation can overwhelm him.
whyNot.2: Doing it for him does not support independence.
whyNot.3: Medical terms make information less accessible.
